overview: This atlas label is an umbrella for parts of the Southeast Asian archipelago between 1492 and 1650, not modern Malaysia or a single Islamic empire. Its very broad outlines include Demak in Java and Gowa in Sulawesi, reach Timor and initially extend into New Guinea. They exclude several famous capitals, including Malacca, Johor Lama, Brunei, Banda Aceh and Banten. Neither common government nor uniform religious affiliation can be read from that shape. The examples below focus on Java and Sulawesi, with neighboring comparisons identified separately; named sultanates retain their own histories.

periods.title: An archipelago of distinct societies
periods.summary: The imported record begins in 1492. Demak’s mosque preserves a Javanese architectural tradition associated with the growing Muslim courts of Java.

periods.title: Ports and shifting courts
periods.summary: After Portugal captured Malacca, its ruling court re-established itself along the Johor River. This neighboring development does not make Johor the ruler of the entire imported outline.

periods.title: Gowa and Talloq adopt Islam
periods.summary: The rulers of Gowa and Talloq embraced Islam in 1605. Their maritime center at Makassar connected local political power to long-distance exchange; 1650 is this atlas record’s cutoff.

items.text: Demak’s Great Mosque has a three-tiered roof, four principal support posts and an open veranda. Its architecture gave Muslim worship a recognizably Javanese setting. Local accounts connect the building with Raden Fatah and the Wali Songo religious teachers, and interpret a turtle emblem as the year 1479. Those foundation traditions should be distinguished from dates of later repairs and surviving timber.

In 1975, archaeologists surveyed Tridonorejo, Moro Demak and Wonosalam. They found roof tiles, bowls, water vessels called kendi, beads and pieces of Chinese and Vietnamese ceramics dated to the fourteenth through sixteenth centuries. These modest fragments bring homes and exchange into view alongside royal stories. Excavation at Tridonorejo also uncovered settlement remains, including building fragments and shells.

Gowa’s growth involved deliberate building. The ruler Tumaparisi Kallonna moved its center from Tamalate to Somba Opu, developed a wharf and ordered an earthen wall around the palace in 1525. A defended coastal capital brought royal authority closer to ships and cargo. The Indonesian archaeological service identifies this port as an important meeting place for traders from different parts of the archipelago.

Gowa and neighboring Talloq had separate ruling houses and a close political partnership. Together they headed a wider federation extending beyond southern Sulawesi. Their power depended on armed forces, fortifications and diplomacy as well as commerce. Historian Tristan Mostert stresses that Makassar was a seat of regional government, not simply a market where ships happened to stop.

Commercial rivalry could turn violent. The Dutch East India Company, or VOC, sought control of the spice trade, while Gowa-Talloq pursued its own regional ambitions. In 1615, departing Dutch traders tried to seize Gowan dignitaries as hostages, killing some people and taking others captive. Local political rivalries and European alliances helped shape the conflict.

In 1605, the rulers of Talloq and Gowa adopted Islam, taking the names Sultan Abdullah Awalul Islam and Sultan Alauddin. This was a change at particular courts, not the simultaneous conversion of everyone across the islands. Gowa’s early harbor-building and political expansion had already begun before its ruler became Muslim.

Makassar’s court annals recorded marriages, births and deaths as matters of public importance. An entry in 1631 names I Taniq, a daughter born to a wife of Daeng Kalula. Such notices reveal family connections around the court, although ordinary households rarely received comparable attention in this record.

A royal hall built in 1631 was named Macciniqdanggang, or “Watching Trade.” The ruler stayed there, linking court life with commercial activity. The same year’s annals also recorded a ban on paying interest on debts: buying, borrowing and religious rules could meet in everyday transactions.

Gowa-Talloq’s intellectual curiosity could generate an enormous shopping request. In 1644, its statesman Pattingalloang ordered geographical and scientific equipment through the VOC, intending to pay for it. His requested globe would have been more than 1.3 meters across, roughly twice the diameter of the largest standard Blaeu globes then made in the Netherlands. Finding desk space might have been a challenge.

Part of that order was sent to Makassar in February 1648: a world map described in Spanish, a four-volume Latin atlas, a burning glass and two telescopes. These objects offered ways to study distant places and optics. They document an unusually well-connected court’s interests, rather than a standard school curriculum for children throughout the islands.

sections.title: Water, food and a line of writing

items.text: Banten, west of this record’s outline, offers a useful neighboring comparison. Its Tasikardi lake was built under Maulana Yusuf, who ruled from 1570 to 1580, to help supply fields and the palace. An island initially served as a retreat for his mother and later as a royal family recreation place. The same landscape could support crops, contemplation and an outing.

The Banten water system also included terracotta pipes and three stations where water settled and passed through sand and palm fiber before reaching the palace. Archaeologists can trace practical efforts to improve water clarity. The surviving system accumulated over time, so every filter cannot be assigned to the lake’s sixteenth-century foundation, nor does clearer water prove modern standards of safety.

Later archaeology at Banten connects cooking with cultural exchange. In deposits studied across the seventeenth to early nineteenth centuries, Dutch residents used locally made cooking pots and lids; archival records also show a shift from bread toward rice. Hired cooks and local women preparing household meals helped transmit techniques. Much of this evidence extends beyond 1650, but it shows how political encounters continued around the stove.

For a Makassarese language sample, Cummings prints “naniaq bosi kontu banning,” translated “there was rain like thread,” under 2 May 1631. This is modern Roman transliteration, not a picture of the script. His principal manuscript, VT 25, is dated 1874 and uses Arabic-derived serang writing; it preserves earlier annals. Another copy says stones instead of thread, a reminder that copied words can change.

Malacca and Johor must also stay distinct. In neighboring territory beyond this polygon, the Portuguese conquest of Malacca in 1511 displaced its court, whose rulers rebuilt their authority along the Johor River. A dynasty could continue after losing a capital. Aceh and Brunei likewise have separate atlas records; this plural label is not a reason to merge their courts or populations.

ending.text: There was no single fall of these “states” in 1650: that is an atlas cutoff. Gowa’s control of Makassar was broken later, in the war of 1666 to 1669, by the VOC and local allies led by Arung Palakka. Other courts and communities followed different paths, which this regional label cannot reduce to one conquest.
